sentences: Meticulous record-keeping saved the department when the inquiry finally arrived.
He was meticulous about the footnotes and vague about the argument.
The third day tested everyone's mettle and revealed two natural leaders.
Mettle and metal were once the same word, which the metaphor still remembers.
The mettlesome young lawyer took the case nobody senior would touch.
A mettlesome horse is admired by everyone except the person riding it.

microcosm.definition: a small world representing a larger one
sentences: The village was a microcosm of the country's argument about itself.
A departmental meeting is a microcosm of every political system ever devised.
His grave mien at the door told them the news before he spoke.
She kept a cheerful mien through a week that deserved none.
Transplanted from his milieu, the charm stopped working entirely.
The novel captures a literary milieu that lasted about four years.

militate.definition: to work against or in favor of something
sentences: Everything about the timetable militated against actually finishing the work.
Militate against is to argue against; mitigate is to soften. They are not the same verb.

milk.definition: to exploit for all it is worth
sentences: He milked the anecdote for three minutes past its natural life.
The franchise was milked until audiences finally stopped turning up.
The harmless snake mimics a venomous one and is left alone by everything.
He mimicked the accent so well that nobody noticed until he laughed.
His mincing delivery made a plain instruction sound like an insult.
She used no mincing words and none were needed.
The minute differences between the samples turned out to be the whole finding.
He gave a minute account of a journey that had taken twelve minutes.
The project was mired in approvals for so long that the technology changed.
Mired in detail, the committee lost sight of what it had been asked.
The typo caused general mirth and one very quiet resignation.
There was no mirth in the room, only the sound of people waiting.
The misanthrope volunteered at the animal shelter and got on famously.
A misanthrope in a small village is a tourist attraction.
His misanthropic column ran for twenty years and was widely loved.
Misanthropic on Monday and cheerful by Thursday is just a normal week.

misappropriate.definition: to take dishonestly for one's own use
sentences: Funds were misappropriated over eleven years in amounts too small to flag.
He misappropriated the phrase and the credit in a single paragraph.
A single sentence was misconstrued and cost two weeks of clarification.
Do not misconstrue silence as agreement; it is usually exhaustion.
The miscreants were identified from a photograph and a very distinctive coat.
Miscreant once meant unbeliever, and drifted into general wrongdoing.

miser.definition: one who hoards money and hates spending
sentences: The miser left three million pounds and a house with no working heating.
Miser shares a root with miserable, which is an ancient piece of moralizing.
The miserly budget for the project produced miserly results, to universal surprise.
He was miserly with praise and lavish with corrections.
"Rush hour" is a misnomer for something that lasts three hours and involves no rushing.
Calling it a working group was a misnomer on both counts.

misogynist.definition: one who hates or despises women
sentences: The misogynist's memoir accidentally documented his own career decline.
Misogynist is from Greek roots meaning hatred of women, and the word carries no ambiguity.

missive.definition: a letter, especially a formal one
sentences: A four-page missive from head office announced a policy in one sentence.
The missive arrived by courier, which told everyone how serious it was.

mite.definition: a very small amount or creature
sentences: He was a mite optimistic about the timeline, by roughly a year.
The widow's mite was tiny and, the parable insists, the largest gift given.
Planting the embankment mitigated the flooding without preventing it.
Mitigate softens a bad thing; militate argues against one.

mode.definition: a way or manner of doing something
sentences: The department switched into crisis mode, which mainly meant longer meetings.
Mode of transport, mode of address, mode in statistics — one word, three careers.
A modest proposal, in Swift's hands, was neither.
The modest raise was accompanied by an immodest description of it.
A modicum of preparation would have prevented the entire disaster.
He asked for a modicum of respect and received the minimum viable amount.
The modish jargon of the report dates it precisely to 2014.
Modish theories arrive with conferences and leave without obituaries.
Nothing mollified the residents except an actual apology, which took two years.
He tried to mollify her with flowers and made an excellent situation worse.

molt.definition: to shed feathers, skin, or shell
sentences: The crab molts its shell and hides for a week while the new one hardens.
The company molted three names in five years and kept the same problems.
A decision of great moment was taken by four people on a Friday afternoon.
The moment passed and nobody moved to reclaim it.
A momentary lapse in attention put the wrong figure into the final table.
The relief was momentary and the paperwork was not.
He kept a monastic routine: one desk, one meal, no telephone.
The monastic silence of the reading room ended when the café opened downstairs.
Monetary policy moved slowly and the prices did not.
The monetary cost was manageable; the reputational one was not.
The monotonous drone of the presentation put three people visibly to sleep.
Monotonous work is bearable with company and unbearable alone.
The monotony of the coastline was broken once, by a lighthouse and a sheep.
Monotony is what makes a five-hour flight longer than a five-hour hike.
The question became moot when the building was sold in March.
Whether it was moot or crucial depended entirely on which side you were on.
The contract dragged them into a morass of subclauses and cross-references.
A morass is a swamp, and the metaphor keeps every bit of the mud.
A moratorium on new hires lasted eleven months and cost two departments their best candidates.
The moratorium on drilling expired quietly on a bank holiday.

morbid.definition: unhealthily preoccupied with death or gloom
sentences: He took a morbid interest in the accident statistics of his own commute.
Morbid curiosity is why the crash makes the front page and the recovery does not.
Her mordant wit made the obituary the most-read piece of the year.
Mordant comes from biting, which is exactly how the humor lands.
The plan was late; moreover, it was based on figures from a previous decade.
"Moreover" in a letter usually signals the paragraph that actually matters.

mores.definition: the accepted customs of a community
sentences: The mores of the office were never written down and were enforced ruthlessly.
Changing laws is easier than changing mores, which is why one lags the other.
The moribund industry was revived by a technology it had spent a decade dismissing.
A moribund committee still meets; that is how you tell it is moribund and not dead.
He grew morose after the verdict and cheerful the day the appeal was filed.
The morose waiter delivered excellent food with visible regret.

morph.definition: to change gradually into something else
sentences: The support group morphed into a lobbying organization over four years.
The complaint morphed, with each retelling, into a much better story.
It mortified him to be corrected by someone he had taught.
Mortify literally means to make dead, which is roughly how embarrassment feels.
Motes of dust hung in the projector beam like a small weather system.
The parable warns about the mote in your brother's eye and the beam in your own.

mountebank.definition: a charlatan who sells false remedies
sentences: The mountebank sold a tonic containing sugar, alcohol, and confident phrasing.
Mountebanks mounted a bench to draw a crowd, which is where the word comes from.

mulct.definition: to fine or swindle out of money
sentences: Investors were mulcted of their savings by a fund with excellent stationery.
The court mulcted him a sum that was, for him, a rounding error.
The problem is multifaceted, which is the polite way to say nobody knows where to start.
A multifaceted career sounds better in a eulogy than it feels at the time.
His multifarious interests filled a house and emptied a bank account.
The multifarious duties of the role were listed on four pages and performed by one person.
A multitude of small errors produced one large and entirely predictable failure.
Charity, says the proverb, covers a multitude of sins.
The mundane detail of the timetable turned out to be the key to the whole case.
Mundane means "of the world," which is either an insult or a description.
A munificent bequest funded the wing and a decade of arguments about its name.
Munificent giving in public is sometimes matched by private meanness.
He mused aloud about resigning and was taken seriously by the wrong person.
She mused for a week and acted in a morning.
She mustered enough support to force a vote and lost it by two.
He could not muster the enthusiasm to finish a sentence about it.

muted.definition: subdued in sound, color, or reaction
sentences: The muted response to the announcement was itself the story.
A muted palette makes a small room feel considerably larger.
The mutiny began over food and ended with a change of management.
Most mutinies are about conditions; the flags come later.
The myopic focus on this quarter cost the company the next decade.
Myopic is literally nearsighted, which is exactly the metaphor intended.
The myriad small kindnesses of that week are what she actually remembers.
Myriad was originally exactly ten thousand, which is disappointingly specific.
The nadir came in March, when even the optimists stopped forecasting.
Nadir is the point directly beneath you; zenith is directly above.
It was naive to assume the deadline meant the same thing to both parties.
Naive questions from a newcomer are the most valuable thing in any meeting.
The narcissist described the disaster mostly in terms of how it had affected him.
Narcissus fell in love with a reflection and gave psychology a permanent word.
The nascent industry had four companies and one very optimistic trade association.
A nascent friendship survives disagreement better than an established one sometimes does.
A natty bow tie made him identifiable in every photograph for forty years.
He arrived natty and left, after the storm, considerably less so.
The strategy was nebulous enough that every department read it as approval.
A nebulous complaint is impossible to answer and impossible to dismiss.
The nefarious scheme required nine accomplices and collapsed under its own logistics.
Nefarious purposes are usually simpler and duller than the word suggests.
One line in the appendix negated the entire conclusion.
The gains were negated by an exchange rate nobody had modeled.
The garden flourished under benign neglect and died under enthusiastic attention.
Neglect ruins buildings more thoroughly and more cheaply than vandalism.
The court found the operator negligent in a way that four inspections had not.
Negligent is careless with legal consequences attached.
The risk was described as negligible by people who would not bear it.
A negligible daily cost becomes a substantial annual one.
Every generation's neologisms are the next generation's plain English.
The neologism was mocked for a decade and printed in the dictionary in the eleventh year.
The neophyte asked the question the veterans had stopped noticing.
Neophyte means newly planted, which is a gentler image than beginner.

net.definition: to obtain or gain as clear profit
sentences: The sale netted less than the auction fees, which the family discovered afterward.
Six months of negotiation netted a single sentence of agreement.
The comparison to his predecessor visibly nettled him.
The plant stings and the verb has kept every bit of the sensation.
The nettlesome question of who pays was deferred to a subcommittee.
A nettlesome detail in the contract delayed everything by three weeks.
The acid was neutralized before anyone noticed the spill.
Their best striker was neutralized by a defender who simply never left him.
The evidence was thin; nevertheless, the policy went ahead.
Nevertheless is the hinge on which most academic paragraphs turn.
The city was the nexus of three trade routes and one very profitable tax.
The nexus between funding and findings is exactly what disclosure rules exist for.

nicety.definition: a fine detail or subtle distinction
sentences: The niceties of protocol delayed a rescue by forty minutes.
He observed every nicety of etiquette and none of the deadlines.

nihilism.definition: the belief that nothing has meaning or value
sentences: The novel's nihilism is undercut by how carefully it is written.
Cheerful nihilism is more common than the philosophical kind and much easier to live with.

nihilist.definition: one who rejects all values and meaning
sentences: The self-described nihilist showed up on time to every single meeting.
Nineteenth-century nihilists in Russia were revolutionaries first and philosophers second.

nimble.definition: quick and light in movement or thought
sentences: A nimble competitor took the market while the incumbent held a strategy retreat.
Nimble fingers and a nimble mind rarely arrive in the same person.
It was a noble gesture and a catastrophic financial decision.
Noble gases refuse to react with anything, which is either aloofness or good taste.
The noisome bins outside the window ended the summer of open windows.
Noisome has nothing to do with noise, which trips up nearly everyone.

nominal.definition: in name only; very small in amount
sentences: He was the nominal head of a department that a deputy actually ran.
A nominal fee of one pound made the transfer legally a sale.
He was nonchalant about the deadline in a way that alarmed everyone else.
Nonchalant means literally not heating up, which is a nice image for cool.
He was dismissed as a nonentity by people who worked for him within a decade.
The committee was chaired by a nonentity, which suited everybody with real interests.
The question nonplussed a speaker who had answered forty harder ones.
Nonplus is Latin for "no more," as in nothing further can be said.
He looked nonplused for a second and then answered perfectly.
American usage has begun to make nonplused mean unbothered, which is the opposite.
The audience was nonplussed by an ending nobody could reconcile with the beginning.
Being nonplussed is a state in which no reply presents itself.

normative.definition: concerning what ought to be, not what is
sentences: The paper slid from a descriptive claim to a normative one without warning.
Normative grammar tells you what to say; descriptive grammar records what people do.
The conference offered nostrums for a problem nobody had diagnosed.
Every economic crisis produces a fresh supply of confident nostrums.

notion.definition: an idea or belief, often vague
sentences: He had a notion that the archive held something, and he was right after eleven months.
The notion that meetings improve decisions has survived remarkably little evidence.
The book's notoriety did more for sales than any of its actual merits.
Notoriety is fame that arrives with a warning label.
Notwithstanding the objections, the plan proceeded on schedule.
The clause begins "notwithstanding anything to the contrary," which lawyers use to win in advance.
The approach was novel in 1962 and is standard practice now.
A novel solution to an old problem usually means somebody read outside the field.
Noxious fumes closed the road for a day and the factory for a decade.
The noxious atmosphere in the department outlasted three managers.
The nuance was lost in translation and started an international incident.
Argument on the internet is the systematic destruction of nuance.

nullify.definition: to make legally void or ineffective
sentences: A procedural error nullified two years of proceedings.
The gains were nullified by a change nobody had bothered to read.

numinous.definition: suggesting the presence of the divine
sentences: The cathedral at dusk has a numinous quality no photograph has captured.
Numinous describes the feeling that something larger is present, whatever you believe it is.
The landlord was obdurate about the rent and vague about the boiler.
Obdurate means hardened, which is what happens to a position defended too long.
The ritual obeisance to the founder opened every annual meeting.
Obeisance is deference performed where others can see it.
The report obfuscated a simple overspend across nine pages of tables.
To obfuscate is to darken, which is exactly the intent.

objective.definition: based on facts, not personal feelings
sentences: The objective account pleased nobody and has aged the best.
Being objective about your own work is a skill nobody fully acquires.
The editor objurgated the whole newsroom for an error one person had made.
Objurgate is scolding that has put on a very formal coat.
The obliging librarian found in four minutes what the catalogue had hidden for years.
An obliging colleague ends up doing everyone's least favorite task.
An oblique reference in the preface was the only acknowledgment she ever received.
He gave an oblique answer that was, on the fourth reading, a refusal.
He walked through the argument entirely oblivious that it concerned him.
Oblivious to the time, she worked until the cleaners arrived.
The obloquy that followed the verdict lasted longer than the sentence did.
Obloquy is being spoken against, loudly and in public.
The summary obscured a finding that the raw data made obvious.
Fog obscured the runway and the entire schedule with it.
The obsequious manner he used with superiors vanished the moment he faced staff.
Obsequious praise tells you about the speaker's fear, not your merit.

obsolete.definition: no longer in use or useful
sentences: The format was obsolete within four years and the archive was on it.
Nothing is obsolete until the last person who can repair it retires.
The obstinate stain outlasted four cleaners and one carpet.
Obstinate about the wrong thing costs more than being wrong about it briefly.
An obstreperous minority delayed the vote by two hours and lost it anyway.
The obstreperous toddler on the flight was, in fairness, the most honest passenger.
The obstructionists on the committee never voted no; they simply requested more information.
Every obstructionist describes themselves as prudent.

obtain.definition: to acquire; to be in force
sentences: The same rules obtain in both jurisdictions, which is unusual and convenient.
He obtained a copy from an archive that officially had none.
He obtruded his opinion into a conversation that had been going well.
The scaffolding obtrudes on a view the guidebook still prints.
He was being deliberately obtuse, which is more irritating than being genuinely slow.
An obtuse angle is blunt, and so is the insult.
A single sentence in the contract obviated three years of potential litigation.
Good design obviates the instruction manual.
The artery was partially occluded, which explained everything the patient had ignored.
Cloud occluded the eclipse for everyone except one field in Cornwall.
The occult meaning of the poem was invented entirely by its critics.
In medicine, occult blood is simply blood you cannot see.
Comparisons are odious, says the proverb, usually quoted by whoever came second.
The odious task of firing the team fell to the one person who had defended it.
The odium attached to the decision outlived everyone who had made it.
He accepted the odium of the unpopular reform and the credit for none of its benefits.
An offhand remark in the corridor became the department's policy for six years.
His offhand manner made people think he had not prepared, which he had, obsessively.
An officious steward moved four people who were in exactly the right seats.
Officious is not official: one is meddling, the other is authorized.
The savings were offset entirely by the cost of achieving them.
Planting trees to offset a flight is arithmetic that works better on paper.

olfactory.definition: relating to the sense of smell
sentences: Olfactory memory bypasses reason entirely, which is why one smell can undo a decade.
The olfactory bulb sits closer to the memory centers than any other sense's wiring.
The ominous silence from the supplier lasted three days and then explained itself.
An ominous sky over a cricket match is the most English form of suspense.
The advertisement was omnipresent for a month and forgotten by the next one.
Dust in that workshop was omnipresent and, the owner insisted, structural.
The narrator's omniscience is what lets the novel see four rooms at once.
Committee members occasionally mistake seniority for omniscience.
The omniscient narrator tells you what the dog is thinking, which is the whole appeal.
Nobody is omniscient, though the tone of certain emails suggests otherwise.
The onerous reporting requirements consumed more time than the work being reported.
An onerous clause is one that only becomes visible when invoked.

onset.definition: the beginning of something, often unpleasant
sentences: The onset of symptoms was gradual enough that nobody dated it correctly.
At the onset of winter the pipes announced their opinions.
The pricing structure was deliberately opaque and profitable for exactly that reason.
His motives remained opaque to colleagues who had known him for twenty years.
He opined at length on a subject he had encountered that morning.
The columnist opines; the reporter reports. Readers rarely distinguish them.

opportunism.definition: exploiting chances without regard to principle
sentences: The sudden conversion to the cause was opportunism with excellent timing.
Opportunism is called agility when it succeeds.

oppress.definition: to keep down by unjust force
sentences: The regime oppressed a minority for forty years and denied it for fifty.
The heat oppressed the whole city until the storm on Thursday.
The opprobrium heaped on the decision made reversing it impossible.
Opprobrium in the press lasts a week; opprobrium in a small town lasts generations.
The optimal route existed only in a model with no traffic and no weather.
Optimal is not the same as good; it is merely the best available.

optimum.definition: the most favorable condition or amount
sentences: The optimum for growth turned out to be three degrees cooler than assumed.
Somewhere between too little and too much lies an optimum nobody has measured.
The opulence of the lobby was funded by the austerity of every other floor.
Opulence photographs beautifully and is exhausting to live in.
The opulent dining room seated forty and was used twice a year.
Opulent taste on a modest budget produces something worse than either.
The funeral oration lasted forty minutes and mentioned the deceased for six.
A great oration changes a room; a good memo changes a policy.

oratorio.definition: a large sacred musical work for voices and orchestra
sentences: The oratorio requires two hundred performers and is staged, therefore, at Christmas.
An oratorio is an opera that stands still, which suits its subject matter.

ordain.definition: to decree officially; to confer holy orders
sentences: The charter ordained that the fund could never be spent, only its interest.
She was ordained in a chapel that had opposed ordaining women for a century.
The ornate ceiling distracted from a room that was otherwise badly proportioned.
His ornate prose takes three clauses to admit it does not know.
The ornery old boiler worked perfectly whenever the engineer was in the room.
Ornery is a worn-down pronunciation of "ordinary," which is a strange journey for a word.
His orotund delivery made a weather forecast sound like a state funeral.
Orotund means round-mouthed, which is exactly what the voice is doing.
The orthodox treatment worked for most patients and nobody investigated the rest.
Today's orthodox position was somebody's heresy within living memory.

oscillate.definition: to swing back and forth; to waver
sentences: Policy oscillated between two positions for four years and arrived at neither.
He oscillated between confidence and panic on roughly a nine-day cycle.
The guidelines ossified into rules that nobody could remember the reason for.
Cartilage ossifies into bone, and so, apparently, do committees.
The ostensible reason was cost; the actual reason was in an email from March.
The ostensible leader was chairing the meeting; the real one was taking notes.
Children learn nouns ostensively: someone points and says the word.
An ostensive definition works for "red" and fails badly for "justice."

ostentatious.definition: showy in an attempt to impress
sentences: The ostentatious watch told everyone the time and one other thing.
Ostentatious modesty is the most expensive kind of showing off.
Ostracism in Athens was voted on with broken pottery and lasted ten years.
Social ostracism does the work that formal punishment cannot.
He was ostracized for reporting the fraud and vindicated four years later.
To ostracize someone slowly is crueler than doing it at once.

oust.definition: to force out of a position
sentences: The founder was ousted by a board he had personally chosen.
Ousting a leader is easy; deciding on the next one is where it fails.
The outlandish claim turned out to be true, which is the worst outcome for a skeptic.
Outlandish once meant simply foreign, which says a good deal about history.

outskirts.definition: the outer edges of a town
sentences: The factory was built on the outskirts and the town grew around it within a generation.
Everything interesting in that city happens on the outskirts.
Demand outstripped supply within a week and the price tripled.
Her ambition outstripped the job, which everyone but the employer noticed.
An overbearing chair turns a committee into an audience.
He was overbearing in meetings and, oddly, courteous in writing.
The scandal overshadowed a budget that was, for once, genuinely interesting.
Her older brother's record overshadowed a career that was, on the numbers, better.
There was no overt threat, which is what made the letter so effective.
Overt discrimination is rarer and easier to prove than the other kind.
His overweening confidence survived four failures and did not survive the fifth.
Overweening ambition is the standard diagnosis for anyone who tried and missed.
The overwrought prose in the final chapter undoes the restraint of the first ten.
She was overwrought by midnight and entirely composed by the hearing.

pacifist.definition: one opposed to war and violence
sentences: The pacifist served four years driving ambulances under fire.
Being a pacifist in wartime requires a different courage, and usually a prison sentence.
A biscuit pacified the toddler and postponed the argument by nine minutes.
The region was pacified, which is a word armies use for something else entirely.

paean.definition: a song or expression of praise
sentences: The review was less criticism than paean, which made readers suspicious.
The book is a paean to a landscape that has since been built on.

painstaking.definition: done with great care and effort
sentences: Painstaking reconstruction of the wreck took nine years and answered the question in one paragraph.
Painstaking work looks effortless, which is why it is so poorly rewarded.

palatable.definition: acceptable in taste or to the mind
sentences: The truth was made palatable by being delivered in the third person.
Hospital food is designed to be palatable and manages, at best, to be warm.

palatial.definition: spacious and splendid like a palace
sentences: After the shared office, a room with a door felt palatial.
The palatial headquarters were completed a year before the layoffs began.
After all the palaver about the venue, the meeting was held online.
The palaver of the visa process took longer than the trip itself.

palimpsest.definition: something reused with traces of what came before
sentences: The city is a palimpsest: Roman road, medieval lane, Victorian sewer, modern cycle path.
Archimedes' lost treatise survived because a monk scraped the parchment and wrote prayers over it.
The news cast a pall over a celebration that had been planned for a year.
A pall is the cloth over a coffin, which is where the gloom comes from.
The grant palliated the crisis and left every underlying cause untouched.
Palliative care treats the person when the disease can no longer be treated.
The pallid imitation made everyone appreciate the original.
He looked pallid under the strip lighting, as everybody does.

palpable.definition: so intense as to seem touchable
sentences: The relief in the room was palpable and lasted about four minutes.
Palpable means literally able to be felt by hand, which doctors still use it for.
His heart palpitated at the sight of the envelope, which contained a leaflet.
The word is used mainly by hearts and by people describing hearts.

panacea.definition: a supposed cure for all problems
sentences: Technology was offered as a panacea and delivered a slightly faster version of the same problem.
Panacea was the Greek goddess of universal remedy, and business is still invoking her.
She handled the collapse with a panache that made the story bearable.
Panache was originally a plume on a helmet, worn to be seen.
The introduction was a panegyric so long the speaker had to shorten his talk.
A panegyric tells you more about the occasion than about its subject.
The full panoply of state ceremony was deployed for a visit lasting ninety minutes.
A panoply was originally a complete suit of armor.

parable.definition: a short story with a moral lesson
sentences: The whole affair became a parable about what happens when nobody reads the contract.
A parable teaches by indirection, which is why the lesson sticks.
The old paradigm explained everything except the results that mattered.
A paradigm shift is announced far more often than it occurs.
The case is paradigmatic: good intentions, no budget, and one very tired coordinator.
A paradigmatic example is the one that teaches the pattern.
The paradox of the plan was that success would make it unnecessary and unfundable.
A paradox is a truth standing on its head to get attention.
It is paradoxical that adding a lane to the motorway lengthens the journey.
The paradoxical result held up under three replications and one furious rebuttal.

paragon.definition: a perfect example of a quality
sentences: He was held up as a paragon of prudence right until the audit.
Nobody wants to work beside a paragon.
The paraphernalia of the hobby filled a garage and cost more than the car.
All the paraphernalia of office arrived before the actual authority did.
The budget was pared until only the parts nobody could defend remained.
He pared the essay to half its length and doubled its force.
The parenthetical remark was the only honest sentence in the report.
His parenthetical asides ran longer than the main clause they interrupted.
He became a pariah in the industry and a hero in one small town.
The company was a pariah for two years and an acquisition target in the third.
Pay parity was promised in 2009 and audited, for the first time, in 2021.
The currency reached parity with the dollar and the headlines reached hysteria.
A parley was arranged on a bridge that belonged to neither side.
The parley lasted an hour and the ceasefire lasted three days.
The debate was parochial: four streets arguing while the region emptied.
Parochial means of the parish, which is precisely the scale of the concern.
The parody was funnier than the original and, unfortunately, indistinguishable from it.
By the fourth season the show had become a parody of itself.
She parried the question with another question and the interview moved on.
He parried three attacks and lost to the fourth, which was a chair.
The parsimonious grant covered travel to the archive and not the return trip.
In science, a parsimonious explanation is a compliment: fewest assumptions wins.
A partial account of a partial recording produced a completely wrong conclusion.
He was partial to strong coffee and partial in every judgment involving his own department.
His partiality for one supplier survived three procurement reviews.
She admitted a partiality for old maps and bought four more.
The partisan coverage described two different events happening in the same room.
Partisan also names an armed resistance fighter, which is a rather different loyalty.
The old guard called him a parvenu, which meant he had earned it rather than inherited it.
Every parvenu becomes an establishment figure in about one generation.

passage.definition: a section of text; the act of moving through
sentences: One passage in the letter was quoted so often that the rest disappeared.
The passage of the bill took four years and one very persuasive amendment.
The technique was declared passé in 1998 and revived, triumphantly, in 2016.
Calling something passé is a claim about the speaker's timing, not the thing.
The building is a pastiche of four centuries and belongs to none of them.
A pastiche done well is affectionate; done badly it is merely derivative.
The pastoral scene in the painting was composed entirely in a London studio.
Pastoral poetry is written by people who have never had to milk anything.
The claim was patent nonsense and was repeated in three broadsheets.
It was patent to everyone that the deadline would be missed.
Most bacteria are not pathogenic, which the public health messaging never quite conveys.
The pathogenic strain differed from the harmless one by a handful of genes.
His pathological need to win small arguments cost him large ones.
Pathological in medicine means diseased; in conversation it means you cannot stop.

patriarch.definition: the male head of a family or group
sentences: The patriarch ruled the business until ninety-one and left no succession plan.
Every family photograph has a patriarch and four people trying to leave.
His patrician manner concealed a childhood in a two-room flat.
The patrician families of Rome kept the priesthoods and, therefore, the calendar.

patronize.definition: to treat condescendingly; to support financially
sentences: Do not patronize the audience; they read the same news you did.
He patronized the arts generously and the artists insufferably.
The patronizing explanation of her own research was the last straw.
Nothing is more patronizing than being told to calm down.
There was a paucity of evidence and a surplus of confidence.
The paucity of women in the archive says more about the archivists than the era.
The press treated a peccadillo as a scandal and the scandal as a technicality.
A peccadillo in one culture is a resignation in another.
The smell was peculiar to that corridor and no one ever traced it.
It struck her as peculiar that four people had the same alibi.
He had no pecuniary interest in the outcome and every other kind.
Pecuniary comes from the Latin for cattle, which is what wealth used to be.
